---
title: "Hot and frost days"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")
p_load(tidyverse)

days <- read_csv("data/weather_karlsruhe.csv") |>
  group_by(year = year(date)) |>
  summarize(
    `Hot days (max ≥ 30 °C)` = sum(temp_max >= 30, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Frost days (min < 0 °C)` = sum(temp_min < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_days = n()
  ) |>
  filter(n_days >= 360) |>
  select(-n_days) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "type", values_to = "days")
```

The annual mean in the [anomaly figure on the home page](index.qmd#fig-anomaly) hides how the extremes changed.
@fig-days counts hot and frost days per year, with a smoothed trend, made with ggplot2 as in
[@wickham2023](references.qmd#ref-wickham2023).

```{r}
#| label: fig-days
#| fig-cap: "Hot and frost days per year in Karlsruhe."
days |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = days, colour = type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Days per year", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

As @fig-days shows, frost days became rarer while hot days became more common.
